newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 12.

text.p: NZ First has wrung nine ministerial posts out of National in the new coalition lineup, rising to 11 posts in two years. In a reversal of NZ First's election policy of a 15-member cabinet, there are to be up to 20 ministers in cabinet, with a further six ministers outside cabinet, one more in total than now. Prime Minister Jim Bolger and NZ First leader Winston Peters signed the coalition agreement between their parties on Wednesday. It includes $3 billion in spending on health and education. The coalition agreement specifies a range of state assets -- Electricity Corporation, Contact Energy, Trans Power, NZ Post, TV1, the National Programme, Concert FM -- which will not be sold. Other state-owned enterprises, which include TV2, Coalcorp, MetService, Airways Corporation and Timberlands, are not listed for protection from sale. Page 1.

The public health system has been given its biggest shake-up since the 1993 health reforms, and will get a funding boost of $1.71 billion over the next three years. The coalition government announced on Wednesday it would spend an extra $378 million on health in the next financial year. It will also dismantle some of the key planks of the reforms, including abolishing regional health authorities and replacing crown health enterprises with regional hospital and community services. The new CHEs will not longer be required to be profit-driven. Page 1.

Homeowners, businesses and exporters can look forward to a brighter Christmas after financial markets on Wednesday gave a small cheer to the National-NZ First coalition. Home mortgage and business interest rates are expected to fall after 90-day bank bill rates dropped by half a percent on Wednesday to just under eight percent -- the lowest level in two years. The fall sparked a decline in the dollar which was down three-quarters of a US cent to just under US69.6 cents, helped down by a weaker Australian dollar after interest rates were cut across the Tasman on Wednesday. Page 1.

Labour was rejected by NZ First because it demanded the top seven cabinet jobs and the deputy prime minister and prime minister's post, NZ First deputy leader Tau Henare said on Wednesday. Henare said it was not Labour leader Helen Clark who was to blame for such tough demands, but her deputy Michael Cullen who "shafted" her. He said Labour's offer on policy was not a problem, but it's patronising attitude and grab for the top job lost it the coalition deal. Page 2.

The first New Zealand MMP government has been described in Australia as a coalition where the "tail wags the dog". The new coalition government dominiated the front pages of the Australian and Sydney Morning Herald newspapers. Page 2.

NZ First's campaign promises to roll back foreign investment and "cut immigration to the bone" are absent from the coalition deal. NZ First leader Winston Peters has wrung only token consessions from National on the policies he is most closely identified with. Page 2.
Labour MP Jonathon Hunt is to challenge the coalition government's nominee Doug Kidd for the job of speaker in the new parliament. Page 2.

The $1 billion cap on treaty settlements has disappeared and the Maori affairs polict which saw Winston Peters dumped from the cabinet by Jim Bolger five years ago is back on the agenda as a result of National's coalition deal with NZ First. Page 3.
The adult minimum wage would rise to $7 an hour from $6.375 from March next year, and could go up to $7.50 after an annual review, the government coalition said on Wednesday. Page 3.

Cash-rich brewer DB Group surprised the market on Wednesday with the announcement of a higher than expected $181 million return to shareholders after a capital reduction of shares. It was widely expected that DB would return the $95 million it had in cash reserves at the end of the financial year on September 30. But chairman David Sadler said on Wednesday that DB would gear its balance sheet up to between 20 and 25 percent through borrowings of $60 million to $70 million. He said this level would give a good rating if DB sought one. Page 18.

Guiness Peat Group's foray into DB Group will pay a multi-million-dollar dividend if Wednesday's rise in share price is any indication. The price increased five cents to $1. DB chairman David Sadler announced a capital reduction through the cancellation of three out of every four shares on issue and repayment of 60 cents a share on the three cancelled. Page 18.

The Reserve Bank would remain cautious about inflation despite the broadening of its target band to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent, Massey University banking professor Chris Moore said on Wednesday. The change was made as part of the coalition agreement between National nd NZ First, along with a change to the wording of the bank's objectives in the policy target agreement. Page 18.

The coalition government is tightening up on tax evasion, asset sales, foreign investment in farm land and is giving a boost to exporters and the fishing industry. An expert committee would be set up to look at tax issues such as the use of "tax-driven structures lacking business reality". On the sale of farm land, the government would be require an individual buyer to be a permanent resident or that the purchase by an individual or "otherwise" would make an unspecified "material contribution" to the economy. On trade, there would be an export credit guarantee scheme, with a guarantee line of up to $50 million a year, for a period of three years. Page 18.
